planting.note: Divide established rhizomes in fall into cool, humus-rich forest soil in deep shade; seed germinates erratically over one to two winters, so division is far more reliable.

directions: A sturdier East Asian counterpart to the familiar American blue cohosh, native to Japan, Korea, northeastern China, and the Russian Far East, where it grows in cool, humus-rich forest understory. It emerges with the same blue-green, meadow-rue-like compound foliage but reaches a somewhat taller, more robust habit, with small yellow-green to purplish flowers in early spring followed by exposed, bright-blue, berry-like seeds. Like its American relative, all parts are toxic, so site it away from edible plantings.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in fall into cool, consistently moist, acidic peaty soil in deep shade; resents heat and dry spells.

directions: The only Asian member of the otherwise North American Clintonia genus, ranging from Japan, Korea, and the Russian Far East through China and the Himalayas. Loose racemes of white to pale-lavender, bell-shaped flowers appear above glossy basal leaves in late spring, followed by blackish-blue berries darker than the vivid cobalt of the already-present North American bluebead lily. It requires cool, consistently moist, acidic peaty soil in deep shade and resents heat and dry spells, though it is hardy to well below zero once dormant.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring into deep, moist, humus-rich woodland soil and leave undisturbed afterward, since established plants resent transplanting.

directions: A temperate East Asian relative of trillium and herb Paris, ranging through Japan, Korea, northeastern China, and the Russian Far East, producing a single unbranched stem topped by a precise whorl of 5 to 9 narrow leaves and one terminal flower with thread-like yellow-green segments. Seed is notoriously slow to germinate and best left undisturbed for two seasons in a shaded cold frame. All parts contain steroidal saponins and are toxic if ingested, so site it away from edible plantings.

planting.note: Divide an established rhizome in spring into deep, evenly moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in shade, and leave undisturbed once established.

directions: A collector-grade Himalayan and west Chinese woodlander in the trillium tribe, bearing quiet green-and-yellow flowers above a broad whorl of leaves in spring, followed by purple fruit. Like other Paris species it is slow from seed due to double dormancy, but builds steadily from rhizome division once established. Give it deep, evenly moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in a permanent shaded woodland spot.
